rs.s1.lede: The odor fingerprint of human milk
rs.s3.lede: Reading GC-O-MS results from an electronic nose
rs.s4.lede: From fatty acids back to infant formula
rs.s1.cap: An electronic nose measured 303 human milk samples and 20 groups of animal milk (1,303 in total). Human and animal milk separate clearly, but human milk from six cities overlaps. Maternal lipid and protein intake show a stronger association with the odor fingerprint than region does.
rs.s2.cap: Sensory evaluation and GC-O-MS compare human milk, infant formula and five animal milks, and ROAV identifies the key flavor compounds that set them apart.
rs.s3.cap: Fast electronic-nose signals are used to predict the key flavor compounds found by GC-O-MS: the 14 sensor signals are compressed first, then six models are combined with weights set per compound.
rs.s4.cap: Ranking fatty acids and free amino acids in human milk: linoleic and α-linolenic acid are most strongly associated with its flavor, while free amino acids matter little. This gives a basis for adjusting the fatty acid profile of infant formula.
